Regression and Correlational Analysis in R

Regression Analysis

Regression analysis is a statistical technique used to examine the relationship between one or more independent variables (predictors) and a dependent variable (outcome). It helps to understand how changes in the independent variables are associated with changes in the dependent variable. Regression analysis can be used for prediction, forecasting, and identifying important factors that influence the outcome.

History of Regression Analysis

Regression analysis has a long history dating back to the 19th century. The term “regression” was first introduced by Sir Francis Galton in the late 1800s when he observed that the heights of children tended to regress toward the mean height of their parents. This concept laid the foundation for the development of regression analysis as a statistical method.

Karl Pearson and Ronald Fisher further contributed to the development of regression techniques in the early 20th century, leading to the widespread use of regression analysis in various fields such as economics, social sciences, and natural sciences.

Correlation Analysis

Correlation analysis, on the other hand, is a statistical method used to measure the strength and direction of the relationship between two variables. It quantifies the degree to which changes in one variable are associated with changes in another variable. Correlation analysis does not imply causation; it only indicates the presence and strength of a relationship.

Distinguishing Correlation and Causation

The two concepts of correlation and causation are often confused, but they are distinct. Correlation indicates a statistical association between two variables, while causation implies that changes in one variable directly cause changes in another. It is important to note that correlation does not imply causation, and further research is often needed to establish causal relationships.

Description of the Dataset

mtcars {datasets} R Documentation Motor Trend Car Road Tests

Description

The data was extracted from the 1974 Motor Trend US magazine, and comprises fuel consumption and 10 aspects of automobile design and performance for 32 automobiles (1973–74 models).

Usage mtcars Format A data frame with 32 observations on 11 (numeric) variables.

\[, 1\] mpg Miles/(US) gallon \[, 2\] cyl Number of cylinders \[, 3\] disp Displacement (cu.in.) \[, 4\] hp Gross horsepower \[, 5\] drat Rear axle ratio \[, 6\] wt Weight (1000 lbs) \[, 7\] qsec 1/4 mile time \[, 8\] vs Engine (0 = V-shaped, 1 = straight) \[, 9\] am Transmission (0 = automatic, 1 = manual) \[,10\] gear Number of forward gears \[,11\] carb Number of carburetors

Scatter Plots are Essential Before Regression and Correlation

library ( ggplot2 )

# Scatterplot : Weight vs MPG
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=wt, y=mpg)) +
  geom_point( color ="blue", size =1) +
  geom_smooth( method ="lm", se=TRUE, color ="red") +
  labs (title =" Relationship between Weight and MPG",
         x=" Weight (1000 lbs)", y=" Miles per Gallon ")

** NOte** There is a strong negative correlation between weight and miles per gallon. As the weight of the car increases, the miles per gallon decreases.

Comput Pearson Correlation Analysis in R

# Compute Pearson correlation
cor(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg, method = "pearson")
[1] -0.8676594

Test significance

State the null and alternative hypotheses:

  • H0: There is no significant correlation between weight and miles per gallon (r = 0).
  • H1: There is a significant correlation between weight and miles per gallon (r ≠ 0).

Decision Rule:

  • If the p-value is less than the significance level (commonly set at 0.05), we reject the null hypothesis. Otherwise, we fail to reject the null hypothesis.

Testing the Significance of the Correlation

cor.test(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg, method = "pearson")

    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  mtcars$wt and mtcars$mpg
t = -9.559, df = 30, p-value = 1.294e-10
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.9338264 -0.7440872
sample estimates:
       cor 
-0.8676594

Interpretation: The Pearson correlation coefficient (r) is -0.867, indicating a strong negative correlation between weight and miles per gallon. The p-value is less than 0.05, which means we reject the null hypothesis and conclude that there is a statistically significant correlation between weight and miles per gallon.

When Normality is Violated or Data is Ordinal

# Compute Spearman correlation
cor(mtcars$wt, mtcars $mpg, method = "spearman")
[1] -0.886422
# Test significance
cor.test(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg, method = "spearman")

    Spearman's rank correlation rho

data:  mtcars$wt and mtcars$mpg
S = 10292, p-value = 1.488e-11
alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
sample estimates:
      rho 
-0.886422

SLR Model in R

## Fit Simple Linear Regression
model_slr <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars )
summary(model_slr)

Call:
lm(formula = mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-4.5432 -2.3647 -0.1252  1.4096  6.8727 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  37.2851     1.8776  19.858  < 2e-16 ***
wt           -5.3445     0.5591  -9.559 1.29e-10 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 3.046 on 30 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.7528,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.7446 
F-statistic: 91.38 on 1 and 30 DF,  p-value: 1.294e-10

State the Null and Alternative Hypotheses:

  • H0: There is no statistically significant effect of weight of the car on miles per gallon (the coefficient for weight is equal to zero) at 5% level of significance.

  • H1: There is a statistically significant effect of weight of the car on miles per gallon (the coefficient for weight is not equal to zero) at 5% level of significance.

Simple Linear Regression Equation

\[\text{Equation:} = \hat{MPG} = 37.2851 -5.3445 \times \text{wt}\]

Interpretation: The coefficient for weight (wt) is -5.344, which means that for every 1 unit increase in weight (1000 lbs), the miles per gallon (mpg) decreases by approximately 5.344 units, holding all else constant. The p-value for the weight variable is less than 0.05, indicating that the effect of weight on miles per gallon is statistically significant at 5% level of significance.

Null and Alternative Hypotheses for the Overall Model (F-Test):

  • H0: The overall regression model is not statistically significant (the model does not explain a significant portion of the variance in miles per gallon).

  • H1: The overall regression model is statistically significant (the model explains a significant portion of the variance in miles per gallon).

Decision Rule:

  • If the p-value for the F-test is less than the significance level (commonly set at 0.05), we reject the null hypothesis. Otherwise, we fail to reject the null hypothesis.

Interpretation of F-Test: The F-statistic is 91.38 with a p-value of 1.294e-10, which is less than 0.05. Therefore, we reject the null hypothesis and conclude that the overall regression model is statistically significant, meaning that weight of the car significantly explains the variance in miles per gallon.

Report R-squared and Adjusted R-squared:

  • R-squared: 0.7528
  • Adjusted R-squared: 0.7446 Interpretation:

The R-squared value of 0.7528 indicates that approximately 75.28% of the variance in miles per gallon (mpg) can be explained by the weight of the car (wt). The adjusted R-squared value of 0.7446 accounts for the number of predictors in the model and provides a more accurate measure of the model’s explanatory power. In this case the adjusted R-squared is slightly lower than the R-squared, which suggests that the model is a good fit for the data, but there may be some room for improvement by including additional predictors.

Confidence Intervals for the Coefficients:

confint(model_slr, level = 0.95)
                2.5 %    97.5 %
(Intercept) 33.450500 41.119753
wt          -6.486308 -4.202635

Interpretation: The 95% confidence interval for the intercept (37.2851) ranges from 33.45 to 41.12, which means we are 95% confident that the true intercept value lies within this range. The 95% confidence interval for the weight coefficient (-5.3445) ranges from -6.49 to -4.20, which means we are 95% confident that the true effect of weight on miles per gallon lies within this range. Since the confidence interval for the weight coefficient does not include zero, it further supports the conclusion that weight has a statistically significant effect on miles per gallon at the 5% level of significance.

Prediction Using the SLR Model:

# New data frame
new_car <- data.frame(wt = 3.5)
new_car
   wt
1 3.5

Narrow confidence interval for the mean response

# Predict with Confidence Interval
predict(model_slr, newdata = new_car, 
         interval = "confidence")
       fit      lwr      upr
1 18.57948 17.43342 19.72553

Wider confidence interval for the mean response

# Predict with Prediction Interval ( wider )
predict(model_slr, newdata = new_car ,
        interval = "prediction")
       fit      lwr      upr
1 18.57948 12.25426 24.90469

Estimate the SLR Model

model_htn <- lm(SBP ~ BMI, data = comp_data, level = 0.95)
summary(model_htn)

Call:
lm(formula = SBP ~ BMI, data = comp_data, level = 0.95)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-40.253  -9.940  -0.960   8.247  98.130 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) 92.84148    1.87229   49.59   <2e-16 ***
BMI          0.85717    0.08562   10.01   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 15.16 on 2324 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.04135,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.04093 
F-statistic: 100.2 on 1 and 2324 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

The Equation of the SLR Model

\[\hat{SBP} = 92.84148 + 0.85717 \times BMI\]

Ranges for BMI

  • Normal BMI: 18.5 to 24.9
  • Overweight BMI: 25 to 29.9
  • Obese BMI: 30 or higher

Multiple Linear Regression (MLR) Model

  • Predictors: wt and hp
  • Outcome: mpg

State the Null and Alternative Hypotheses for the MLR Model:

  • H0: There is no statistically significant effect of weight and horsepower on miles per gallon (the coefficients for weight and horsepower are equal to zero) at 5% level of significance.

  • H1: There is a statistically significant effect of weight and horsepower on miles per gallon (the coefficients for weight and horsepower are not equal to zero) at 5% level of significance.

Select of Level of Significance

  • Commonly set at 0.05

Collect the Data

Run the Test (Multple Linear Regression Model)

model_mlr <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars)
summary(model_mlr)

Call:
lm(formula = mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars)

Residuals:
   Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
-3.941 -1.600 -0.182  1.050  5.854 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) 37.22727    1.59879  23.285  < 2e-16 ***
wt          -3.87783    0.63273  -6.129 1.12e-06 ***
hp          -0.03177    0.00903  -3.519  0.00145 ** 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 2.593 on 29 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.8268,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.8148 
F-statistic: 69.21 on 2 and 29 DF,  p-value: 9.109e-12

The Equation of the MLR Model

\[\hat{MPG} = 37.22727 - 3.877 \times \text{wt} - 0.031 \times \text{hp}\]

Decision Rule for the MLR Model:

If the p-value for a predictor is less than the significance level (commonly set at 0.05), we reject the null hypothesis for that predictor. Otherwise, we fail to reject the null hypothesis for that predictor.

Interpretation of the MLR Model:

  • The coefficient for weight (wt) is -3.877, which means that for every 1 unit increase in weight (1000 lbs), the miles per gallon (mpg) decreases by approximately 3.877 units, holding horsepower (hp) constant. The p-value for weight is less than 0.05, indicating that the effect of weight on miles per gallon is statistically significant at 5% level of significance.

  • The coefficient for horsepower (hp) is -0.031, which means that for every 1 unit increase in horsepower, the miles per gallon (mpg) decreases by approximately 0.031 units, holding weight (wt) constant. The p-value for horsepower is less than 0.05, indicating that the effect of horsepower on miles per gallon is statistically significant at 5% level of significance.

Reporyt R-squared and Adjusted R-squared for the MLR Model:

  • An R-squared value of 0.8268 indicates that approximately 82.68% of the variance in miles per gallon (mpg) can be explained by the weight and horsepower of the car. The adjusted R-squared value of 0.8148 accounts for the number of predictors in the model and provides a more accurate measure of the model’s explanatory power. In this case, the adjusted R-squared is slightly lower than the R-squared, which suggests that the model is a good fit for the data, but there may be some room for improvement by including additional predictors or considering interactions between predictors.

  • An adjusted R-squared value of 0.8148 indicates that approximately 81.48% of the variance in miles per gallon (mpg) can be explained by the weight and horsepower of the car, after adjusting for the number of predictors in the model. This suggests that the model has a strong explanatory power, but there may still be some unexplained variance that could potentially be accounted for by including additional predictors or considering interactions between predictors.

Model Diagnostics for the MLR Model

Multicollinearity

Multicollinearity occurs when two or more predictor variables in a multiple regression model are highly correlated with each other. This can lead to unstable estimates of the regression coefficients and make it difficult to determine the individual effect of each predictor on the outcome variable.

library (car)
# Calculate VIF
vif(model_mlr)
      wt       hp 
1.766625 1.766625

Report VIF Values:

  • VIF values for weight (wt) and horsepower is 1.766625 indicating that there is no significant multicollinearity between the predictors in the model. Generally, a VIF value greater than 5 or 10 is considered indicative of high multicollinearity, so in this case, the VIF values suggest that multicollinearity is not a concern for this model.

US economic time series

Description

This dataset was produced from US economic time series data available from https://fred.stlouisfed.org/. economics is in “wide” format, economics_long is in “long” format.

Usage economics

economics_long Format A data frame with 574 rows and 6 variables:

date Month of data collection

pce personal consumption expenditures, in billions of dollars, https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PCE

pop total population, in thousands, https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/POP

psavert personal savings rate, https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PSAVERT/

uempmed median duration of unemployment, in weeks, https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/UEMPMED

unemploy number of unemployed in thousands, https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/UNEMPLOY

An object of class tbl_df (inherits from tbl, data.frame) with 2870 rows and 4 columns.

Marginal Elasticities

model_elasticity <- lm(log(CPI) ~ log(ExchRate) + log(LendIntRates), data = df)
summary(model_elasticity)

Call:
lm(formula = log(CPI) ~ log(ExchRate) + log(LendIntRates), data = df)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-0.3328 -0.1943  0.0154  0.1211  0.5152 

Coefficients:
                  Estimate Std. Error t value            Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)       -0.70426    0.52767  -1.335            0.195053    
log(ExchRate)      1.51494    0.08531  17.758 0.00000000000000635 ***
log(LendIntRates) -0.55204    0.13754  -4.014            0.000544 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.223 on 23 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.9348,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.9291 
F-statistic: 164.8 on 2 and 23 DF,  p-value: 0.00000000000002317

The estimated equation is:

\[\ln(\text{CPI})=-0.7043+1.5149\ln(\text{ExchRate})-0.5520\ln(\text{LendIntRates}).\]

Because both the dependent and independent variables are in logarithms, this is a log-log (double-log) regression model. The coefficients are interpreted as elasticities, not multipliers.

or equivalently,

\[CPI=e^{-0.7043}\times ExchRate^{1.5149}\times LendIntRates^{-0.5520}.\]

Interpretation of the coefficients

1. Exchange Rate Elasticity

The coefficient is

\[\beta_1=1.5149.\]

Interpretation:

Holding lending interest rates constant, a 1% increase in the exchange rate is associated with approximately a 1.515% increase in the Consumer Price Index (CPI).

Since

\[1.515>1,\]

CPI is elastic with respect to the exchange rate.

This suggests that exchange rate depreciation has a more-than-proportional effect on inflation.

2. Lending Interest Rate Elasticity

The coefficient is

\[\beta_2=-0.5520.\]

Interpretation:

Holding exchange rates constant, a 1% increase in lending interest rates is associated with approximately a 0.552% decrease in CPI.

This relationship is inelastic because

\[|{-0.552}|<1.\]

Economically, higher lending rates reduce borrowing and aggregate demand, thereby lowering inflationary pressures.

Statistical significance

Exchange Rate

\[p<0.001\]

Highly significant.

There is very strong evidence that exchange rate movements affect CPI.

Lending Interest Rate

\[p=0.000544\]

Also highly significant.

Higher lending rates significantly reduce inflation.

Goodness of fit

Multiple (R^2)

\[R^2=0.9348\]

Interpretation:

Approximately 93.48% of the variation in CPI is explained jointly by exchange rates and lending interest rates.

Adjusted (R^2)

\[0.9291\]

Since it is very close to (R^2), the model is not overfitting.

Overall model significance

The F-statistic is

\[F=164.8\]

with

\[p=2.317\times10^{-14}.\]

Interpretation:

The model is highly statistically significant, indicating that the explanatory variables jointly provide substantial explanatory power for CPI.

What can you compute from this model?

Unlike a consumption model, you cannot compute the Keynesian multiplier

\[k=\frac{1}{1-MPC},\]

because:

  • there is no consumption variable,
  • there is no income variable, and
  • the coefficients are elasticities, not marginal propensities to consume.

Instead, you obtain:

  • Exchange rate elasticity of inflation = 1.515
  • Lending interest rate elasticity of inflation = −0.552
  • Overall explanatory power ((R^2))
  • Statistical significance of each determinant
  • Predictive equation for CPI
  • Evidence on exchange rate pass-through and the effect of monetary policy (through lending rates)

A suitable interpretation for a research paper

The estimated double-log regression model indicates that the exchange rate has a positive and statistically significant effect on inflation. Specifically, a 1% increase in the exchange rate is associated with an estimated 1.515% increase in the Consumer Price Index (CPI), holding lending interest rates constant. This suggests a highly elastic exchange rate pass-through to domestic prices. Conversely, lending interest rates have a negative and statistically significant effect on inflation, with a 1% increase in lending rates associated with an estimated 0.552% decrease in CPI. The model explains approximately 93.5% of the variation in CPI ((R^2 = 0.9348)), and the overall regression is highly significant ((F = 164.8), (p < 0.001)), indicating that exchange rates and lending interest rates jointly provide a strong explanation of inflation dynamics in the sample.

These are excellent results for illustrating demand elasticity. Since you estimated a double-log demand model, every slope coefficient is an elasticity. This makes the model ideal for teaching and reporting economic concepts.

Your estimated model is

\[\ln(Q)=8.194-1.139\ln(P)+0.753\ln(Y)+0.537\ln(P_s)-0.407\ln(P_c)\]

where:

    1. = Quantity demanded
    1. = Price of the good
    1. = Consumer income

  • (P_s) = Price of substitute goods

  • (P_c) = Price of complementary goods

1. Price Elasticity of Demand

The estimated own-price elasticity is

\[E_p=-1.139.\]

Interpretation

Holding income, substitute prices, and complementary goods’ prices constant, a 1% increase in the price of the good decreases quantity demanded by approximately 1.139%.

Since

\[|E_p|=1.139>1,\]

the demand is price elastic. Consumers are relatively responsive to price changes.

Economic implication

A price increase is likely to reduce total revenue because the percentage decline in quantity demanded exceeds the percentage increase in price.

2. Income Elasticity of Demand

The estimated income elasticity is

\[E_Y=0.753.\]

Interpretation

Holding other variables constant, a 1% increase in consumer income increases quantity demanded by approximately 0.753%.

Since

\[0<E_Y<1,\]

the product is a normal necessity.

Economic implication

Demand increases as consumers become wealthier, but at a slower rate than income growth.

3. Cross-Price Elasticity (Substitute Goods)

The estimated elasticity is

\[E_{Sub}=0.537.\]

Interpretation

A 1% increase in the price of a substitute good increases demand for this product by approximately 0.537%, holding other variables constant.

Because

\[E_{Sub}>0,\]

the goods are substitutes.

Examples

  • Coca-Cola and Pepsi
  • Tea and Coffee
  • Butter and Margarine

Economic implication

If competitors raise their prices, consumers switch to your product.

4. Cross-Price Elasticity (Complementary Goods)

The estimated elasticity is

\[E_{Comp}=-0.407.\]

Interpretation

A 1% increase in the price of a complementary good decreases demand for this product by approximately 0.407%, holding other factors constant.

Because

\[E_{Comp}<0,\]

the goods are complements.

Examples

  • Cars and fuel
  • Printers and ink cartridges
  • Bread and butter

Economic implication

An increase in the price of a complementary product reduces demand for the focal product.

5. Statistical Significance

All explanatory variables have p-values less than 0.001, indicating that price, income, substitute prices, and complementary goods’ prices all have statistically significant effects on quantity demanded.

6. Model Fit

The coefficient of determination is

\[R^2=0.9104.\]

Interpretation

Approximately 91.04% of the variation in quantity demanded is explained by the four explanatory variables.

The adjusted (R^2) of 0.9066 indicates that the model retains very strong explanatory power after accounting for the number of predictors.

7. Overall Model Significance

The overall regression is highly significant:

  • (F = 241.3)
  • (p < 0.001)

This indicates that the explanatory variables jointly provide substantial explanatory power for explaining demand.

Summary Table

Variable Elasticity Economic Interpretation Classification
Price −1.139 1% ↑ in price → 1.139% ↓ in demand Elastic demand
Income 0.753 1% ↑ in income → 0.753% ↑ in demand Normal necessity
Substitute Price 0.537 1% ↑ in substitute’s price → 0.537% ↑ in demand Substitute goods
Complement Price −0.407 1% ↑ in complement’s price → 0.407% ↓ in demand Complementary goods

The model demonstrates several fundamental concepts in demand analysis within a single regression:

  • ✅ Demand function estimation
  • ✅ Own-price elasticity of demand
  • ✅ Income elasticity of demand
  • ✅ Cross-price elasticity of demand (substitutes)
  • ✅ Cross-price elasticity of demand (complements)
  • ✅ Elastic vs. inelastic demand
  • ✅ Normal vs. inferior goods (if income elasticity were negative)
  • ✅ Statistical significance (t-tests and p-values)
  • ✅ Overall model significance (F-test)
  • ✅ Goodness of fit ((R^2) and Adjusted (R^2))

Because it captures nearly all of the core elasticity concepts in one framework, this type of double-log demand model is widely used in econometrics and is an excellent example for classroom demonstrations, assignments, and applied research.
